question: What are vulval varicose veins?

options.A: Benign fluid-filled cysts inside the myometrium of the uterus
options.B: Infections of the Bartholin glands located near the vaginal opening
options.C: Inflammation of the urinary bladder lining caused by bacteria
options.D: Enlarged and dilated blood vessels on the external genitalia

explanation: Spotting swollen, twisted veins on the labia or external parts can look scary, but they are just like varicose veins on the legs—they are simply enlarged blood vessels. You've got this! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h1)

question: When do vulval varicose veins most commonly show up?
explanation: Pregnancy is the peak time for this! The body increases its blood volume and puts extra pressure in the pelvis, which makes these veins pop up. Great job thinking through prenatal changes. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h1)

question: Which hormone is mainly responsible for relaxing blood vessel walls during pregnancy?
explanation: Think of progesterone as the great relaxer of smooth muscles in the body. It helps the body adapt to pregnancy, but it also relaxes vein walls, making them stretch out easily. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h2)

question: How does the growing uterus help cause vulval varicosities?

options.A: It directly damages the external skin of the labia
options.B: It blocks the arterial supply to the perineum
options.C: It releases enzymes that weaken capillary membranes
options.D: It presses on pelvic veins and slows down blood return

explanation: As the baby and uterus grow heavier, they act like a heavy blanket pressing down on the big pelvic veins. This slows down the blood trying to flow back up, causing it to pool below. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h2)

question: Which factor makes a woman more likely to get vulval varicosities in her later pregnancies?
explanation: Multiparity just means having had multiple pregnancies! Each time, the pelvic veins stretch out a bit more, making them more prone to swelling in future pregnancies. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h3)

question: When do expectant mothers usually notice that their vulval varicose veins hurt or ache the most?

options.B: Immediately upon waking up in the morning
options.C: After standing or walking for a long time
options.D: While resting flat on their back

explanation: Gravity is the culprit here! Staying on your feet all day lets blood pool downward, so by evening, the pressure and ache feel much stronger. Rest and elevation are best friends here. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h3)

question: Why is it so important for a nurse to create a private, gentle setting during a perineal check?

options.A: Bright lighting interferes with visualizing superficial blood vessels
options.B: Perineal tissue is too fragile to touch without numbing agents
options.C: Patients frequently feel embarrassed about intimate examinations
options.D: Hospital policy strictly forbids family members from staying

explanation: Checking someone's private areas can feel very vulnerable. As a caring nurse, building trust and keeping things private helps your patient feel safe and respected. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h4)

question: When a patient has vulval varicosities, which other body part should you check as a nurse?
explanation: Since pelvic congestion flows downward, it's very common to see leg varicose veins or swollen ankles accompanying vulval veins. Always look at the whole picture! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h4)

question: Which sleeping position helps take pressure off pelvic veins during pregnancy?
explanation: Lying on the left side moves the heavy uterus off the major blood vessel (inferior vena cava), keeping blood flowing smoothly back to the heart. It's a classic, golden rule of maternity care! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h5)

question: Why should pregnant women with vulval varicosities try hard to avoid constipation?

options.A: Bowel pressure directly blocks the arterial supply to the labia
options.B: Straining during bowel movements increases pelvic venous pressure
options.C: Constipation stops the kidneys from filtering blood properly
options.D: Hard stools can physically puncture the dilated perineal veins

explanation: Straining pushes extra pressure downward into veins that are already stretched to their limit. Encouraging fluids and fiber helps keep things soft and protects those veins! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h5)

question: What is the general rule for how women with vulval varicose veins give birth?

options.A: A scheduled caesarean section is required in every single case
options.B: Labor must be induced early at thirty-six weeks gestation
options.C: Vaginal delivery is usually safe and successful for most women
options.D: Forceps delivery must be used to protect the perineal blood vessels

explanation: Good news! Having vulval varicosities doesn't automatically mean a C-section. Most mothers have safe, normal vaginal deliveries with proper supportive care. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h6)

question: Why do birth attendants need to be extra careful if an episiotomy is done near vulval varicosities?

options.A: Dilated blood vessels tend to bleed much more heavily when cut
options.B: Cutting the skin will cause permanent nerve paralysis in the leg
options.C: Local anaesthetic injections will not work near swollen tissues
options.D: The wound will never heal properly due to poor local hygiene

explanation: Engorged veins are full of blood under pressure. Cutting near them requires extra caution because they can bleed quite heavily. You're building great clinical intuition! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a sign of superficial thrombophlebitis in a vulval vein?

options.A: A firm, tender, cord-like swelling in the tissue
options.B: Mild discomfort when walking or sitting down
options.C: Complete absence of any pain or tenderness
options.D: Localized redness and warmth over the vessel

explanation: When a vein gets inflamed and forms a little clot (thrombophlebitis), it hurts! There is never a 'complete absence' of pain—it's usually tender, warm, and swollen. [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h7)

question: What usually happens to vulval varicose veins after the baby is born?

options.A: They immediately spread upward into the abdominal cavity
options.B: They always turn into permanent open ulcers on the skin
options.C: They remain unchanged for the rest of the woman's life
options.D: They shrink and regress significantly within a few weeks

explanation: Once delivery happens and hormone levels drop back down, the pelvic pressure disappears, and those swollen veins naturally shrink back down. Nature heals wonderfully! [learn more](GNS216_U5_T9#GNS216_U5_T9_h7)
